extracted.intended_audience: public water system operators, state regulators, and drinking water testing laboratories
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory requirements for analytical methods, sampling, laboratory certification, monitoring frequencies, reduced-monitoring criteria, monitoring plans, and compliance calculations for disinfection byproducts and disinfectant residuals in public water systems under EPA Part 141.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of IBR‑approved analytical methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems must measure contaminants and residuals by the EPA, Standard Methods, or ASTM methods listed (or by alternative methods listed in appendix A to subpart C) as indicated in the approved methods tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific method numbers are enumerated for each contaminant (e.g., EPA Method 327.0 Rev 1.1 for Lissamine Green spectrophotometric chlorine dioxide/chlorite; EPA Methods 502.2, 524.2, 551.1 for TTHMs; Standard Methods and ASTM references are cited). Only the listed Online versions that are IBR‑approved may be used. Footnotes specify method-specific requirements (e.g., extraction timing, detector options).

rubrics_metrics.name: Laboratory certification to perform DBP analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses for disinfection byproducts must be conducted by laboratories that have received certification by EPA or the State, except as specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To receive certification a lab must: (i) analyze Performance Evaluation (PE) samples acceptable to EPA or the State at least once during each consecutive 12‑month period for each method requested; (ii) meet acceptance limits described (see separate rubric on PE acceptance limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: PE sample acceptance limits (pre‑April 1, 2007)
rubrics_metrics.description: Until March 31, 2007, in PE sample analyses, the laboratory must achieve quantitative results within the acceptance limit on a minimum of 80% of the analytes included in each PE sample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The acceptance limit is defined as the 95% confidence interval around the PE study mean, bounded by a maximum and minimum acceptance limit of ±50% and ±15% of the study mean.

rubrics_metrics.name: PE sample acceptance limits (beginning April 1, 2007)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning April 1, 2007, laboratories must achieve quantitative results within specified acceptance limits (percent of true value) on PE samples for each analyte.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specified acceptance limits: TTHM individual THMs ±20% (lab must meet all 4 to pass TTHM PE), HAA5 compounds ±40% (must meet 4 of 5 to pass HAA5 PE), chlorite ±30%, bromate ±30%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum reporting levels (MRLs) for DBP analytes
rubrics_metrics.description: Laboratories must report quantitative data for concentrations at least as low as the specified MRLs for all DBP samples analyzed for compliance with §§141.64, 141.135, and subparts U and V.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tables list MRLs such as 0.0010 mg/L for each individual THM, 0.0020 mg/L for monochloroacetic acid, 0.020 mg/L for chlorite, bromate 0.0050 or 0.0010 mg/L (methods 317.0 Rev 2.0, 326.0 or 321.8 require 0.0010). Calibration curve must encompass MRL; labs may report lower concentrations if precision/accuracy criteria met; an MRL check standard (≤110% of MRL) must be analyzed with each batch and its measured concentration must be ±50% of expected value if any field sample in batch <5× MRL.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method‑specific sample handling and holding times
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods specify preservation, extraction timing, filtration, acidification, and analysis holding times for different analytes (e.g., benzene, TOC, DOC, UV254, bromate, chlorite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: HAA LLE samples must be extracted within 14 days; bromate samples preserved with 50 mg ethylenediamine (EDA)/L and analyzed within 28 days; TOC samples must be acidified at collection to pH ≤2 and analyzed within 28 days; DOC samples must be filtered through 0.45 μm as soon as practical (≤48 hours), acidified to pH ≤2 after filtration, inorganic carbon removed, and analyzed within 28 days; UV254 samples filtered 0.45 μm, pH not adjusted, analyzed ≤48 hours.

rubrics_metrics.name: SUVA determination procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: SUVA equals UV254 (m‑1) divided by DOC (mg/L) and must be determined on water prior to addition of disinfectants/oxidants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems must separately measure UV254 and DOC using specified methods; DOC and UV254 samples used to determine SUVA must be taken at the same time and same location; DOC: filter, acidify, analyze within 28 days; UV254: filter, measure at 253.7 nm (may round to 254 nm), analyze ≤48 hours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approved methods for disinfectant residuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Residual disinfectant concentration for free chlorine, combined chlorine (chloramines), total chlorine, and chlorine dioxide must be measured by the approved methods listed (Standard Methods, ASTM, EPA methods) or alternative methods in appendix A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The table identifies which methods are approved for which residual (e.g., Amperometric titration 4500‑Cl D for free/combined/total Cl; DPD colorimetric 4500‑Cl G for free/combined/total Cl; Lissamine Green Spectrophotometric 327.0 Rev 1.1 for ClO2). Footnotes note that free or total chlorine may be used to demonstrate chlorine MRDL compliance and combined or total chlorine for chloramine MRDL.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of DPD colorimetric test kits (State approval)
rubrics_metrics.description: If approved by the State, systems may measure residual disinfectant concentrations using DPD colorimetric test kits for chlorine, chloramines, and chlorine dioxide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State approval is required for using test kits in lieu of laboratory methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional analytical methods for other parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Parameters not in disinfection byproducts/residuals sections must use specified methods or alternatives in appendix A; a party approved by EPA or State must perform these measurements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: alkalinity — all methods allowed in §141.89(a); bromide — EPA Methods 300.0, 300.1, 317.0 Rev 2.0, 326.0, or ASTM D6581‑00; TOC — Standard Methods 5310 B/C/D or EPA Method 415.3 Rev 1.1 with inorganic carbon removal and other sample handling rules; pH and magnesium — all methods allowed in §141.23(k)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: General sampling requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems must take all samples during normal operating conditions and may consider multiple wells drawing from same aquifer as one treatment plant with State approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to monitor according to the monitoring plan is a monitoring violation; failure to monitor can be treated as violation for the entire period covered by an annual average where compliance is based on running annual average; only data collected under the provisions of this subpart may be used to qualify for reduced monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring plan requirement and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Each system required to monitor must develop, implement, maintain, and make available a monitoring plan; Subpart H systems serving >3300 must submit a copy to the State by first reporting date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan must be available for inspection by State and public no later than 30 days after compliance dates in §141.130(b). State may require plan submission and may require changes. Plan must include at least: (1) specific locations and schedules for collecting samples for any parameters in this subpart; (2) how the system will calculate compliance with MCLs, MRDLs, and treatment techniques; (3) if consecutive system approved, plan must reflect entire distribution system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine monitoring frequency and sample locations for TTHM and HAA5
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimum monitoring frequency and sample location requirements for TTHM and HAA5 vary by system type and population served (tables provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Subpart H systems serving ≥10,000: four water samples per quarter per treatment plant, with ≥25% of samples each quarter at locations representing maximum residence time and remaining samples at locations of at least average residence time representing entire distribution system. Systems serving 500–9,999: one water sample per quarter at locations representing maximum residence time. Systems <500: one sample per year in warmest month at location representing maximum residence time. Special provisions for groundwater systems not under direct surface influence are included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increased monitoring when MCL exceeded for TTHM/HAA5
rubrics_metrics.description: If a sample (or annual average) exceeds the MCL, the system must increase monitoring to one sample per treatment plant per quarter at point reflecting maximum residence time until criteria for reduced monitoring are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When increased monitoring is required, compliance calculation rules (including which samples to include) are specified elsewhere; systems electing to sample more frequently must still collect ≥25% of quarterly samples at maximum residence time locations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced monitoring eligibility for TTHM and HAA5
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems may reduce monitoring if they meet monitoring history and water quality criteria (tables provide combinations of population, TOC, and TTHM/HAA5 annual averages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example criteria: Subpart H systems with source water annual average TOC ≤4.0 mg/L and TTHM annual average ≤0.040 mg/L and HAA5 ≤0.030 mg/L may reduce to one sample per plant per quarter at location reflecting maximum residence time (larger systems) or to one sample/year (smaller systems). Special rules for groundwater systems and three‑year monitoring cycles are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source water TOC monitoring to qualify for reduced monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify for reduced TTHM/HAA5 monitoring, subpart H systems not monitoring under paragraph (d) must take monthly TOC samples every 30 days at a location prior to any treatment beginning April 1, 2008 (or earlier if State specifies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Source water TOC running annual average must be ≤4.0 mg/L (based on most recent four quarters) on a continuing basis at each treatment plant to reduce or remain on reduced monitoring. Once qualified, source water TOC monitoring may be reduced to quarterly (every 90 days) at a location prior to treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for remaining on or reverting from reduced monitoring (TTHM/HAA5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems on reduced monitoring may remain if sample averages stay below specified thresholds; exceeding thresholds forces a return to routine monitoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems on reduced schedule may remain as long as the average of all samples taken in the year (for quarterly systems) or the result of the annual sample is ≤0.060 mg/L (TTHM) and ≤0.045 mg/L (HAA5). Systems not meeting these must resume routine monitoring in the next quarter. For ground water systems serving <10,000, higher thresholds (TTHM >0.080 or HAA5 >0.060) trigger increased monitoring. Systems on increased monitoring may return to routine monitoring if after ≥1 year TTHM annual average ≤0.060 and HAA5 ≤0.045. State may also return a system to routine monitoring at State discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chlorite monitoring requirements (systems using chlorine dioxide)
rubrics_metrics.description: Community and nontransient noncommunity systems using chlorine dioxide must conduct chlorite monitoring: daily at entrance and monthly three-sample sets in distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine daily monitoring: take daily samples at entrance; if any daily sample exceeds the chlorite MCL, take additional distribution samples the following day. Monthly monitoring: a three-sample set each month at near‑first‑customer, average residence time, and maximum residence time. Additional monitoring after exceedance: three distribution samples at first customer, average location, and end of distribution. Reduced monitoring: entrance monitoring may not be reduced; distribution monitoring may be reduced to one three-sample set per quarter after one year with no individual exceedance and no triggered additional monitoring; revert to routine if any quarterly three-sample set exceeds MCL or additional monitoring is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bromate monitoring requirements (systems using ozone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Community and nontransient noncommunity systems using ozone must take one sample per month for each treatment plant at the entrance to the distribution system while ozonation is operating under normal conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduced monitoring pre‑2009 allowed if average source water bromide <0.05 mg/L for one year; after April 1, 2009, reduced monitoring allowed only if running annual average bromate ≤0.0025 mg/L based on monthly bromate samples analyzed using Methods 317.0 Rev 2.0, 326.0 or 321.8. Systems that qualified under older provisions may remain on reduced monitoring as long as running annual average of quarterly bromate samples ≤0.0025 mg/L. If running annual average ≥0.0025 mg/L, system must resume routine monthly monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chlorine and chloramine residual monitoring timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Community and non‑transient non‑community systems that use chlorine or chloramines must measure residual disinfectant level in the distribution system at the same point and time as total coliform samples are taken (per specified sections and dates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Until March 31, 2016 follow §141.21 timing; beginning April 1, 2016 follow §§141.854–141.858. Subpart H systems may use residual sampling results from specified sections in lieu of separate sampling. Reduced monitoring for chlorine/chloramines may not be reduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinfectant residual monitoring for chlorine dioxide (routine/additional/reduced)
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems using chlorine dioxide must take daily entrance samples; following an exceedance they must take three distribution samples the next day at specified locations; chlorine dioxide monitoring may not be reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If chlorine dioxide or chloramines are used to maintain residual and there are no booster additions, take three samples as close to first customer as possible at ≥6 hour intervals; with booster chlorination take one sample at first customer, average residence time, and end of distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring requirements for disinfection byproduct precursors (TOC/alkalinity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subpart H systems using conventional filtration must monitor each plant for TOC no later than combined filter effluent turbidity monitoring and must also monitor source water TOC and source water alkalinity as paired samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems must take one paired sample and one source water alkalinity sample per month per plant at normal operating conditions. Reduced monitoring allowed if average treated water TOC <2.0 mg/L for two consecutive years or <1.0 mg/L for one year (reduced to quarterly paired samples); revert to routine monitoring if annual average treated water TOC ≥2.0 mg/L.

rubrics_metrics.name: All samples included in compliance determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: All samples taken and analyzed under provisions of this subpart must be included in determining compliance, even if greater than the minimum required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to monitor is a monitoring violation and may make it impossible to determine compliance; where compliance is based on running annual averages, failure to monitor will be treated as a violation for the entire period covered by the annual average.

rubrics_metrics.name: TTHM and HAA5 compliance calculation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: For quarterly monitoring, compliance is based on a running annual arithmetic average, computed quarterly, of quarterly arithmetic averages of all samples collected as prescribed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For less frequent than quarterly, compliance is based on the average of samples taken that year. If such average exceeds the MCL, the system must increase monitoring to quarterly and is not in violation until it completes one year of quarterly monitoring unless fewer than four quarters already cause the running annual average to exceed the MCL (in which case system is in violation at end of that quarter). Systems increasing to quarterly must include the triggering sample plus following three quarters when calculating compliance. If running annual arithmetic average of any consecutive four‑quarter period exceeds MCL, system is in violation, must notify public (per §141.32 or §141.202) and report to State per §141.134. If PWS fails to complete four consecutive quarters, compliance for last four‑quarter period based on available data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bromate compliance calculation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliance based on running annual arithmetic average, computed quarterly, of monthly samples (or monthly averages if >1 sample per month) collected as prescribed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If average covering any consecutive four‑quarter period exceeds MCL, system is in violation and must notify public (subpart Q) and report to State (§141.134). If PWS fails to complete 12 consecutive months' monitoring, compliance for last four‑quarter period based on available data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chlorite compliance calculation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliance must be based on an arithmetic average of each three‑sample set taken in the distribution system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the arithmetic average of any three‑sample set exceeds the MCL, the system is in violation and must notify the public (subpart Q) and report to the State (§141.134).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinfectant residuals compliance and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Chlorine and chloramine compliance must be based on running annual arithmetic average, computed quarterly, of monthly averages of all samples; exceeding MRDL for any consecutive four‑quarter period constitutes a violation requiring public notification and reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If systems switch between chlorine and chloramines, compliance includes results for both disinfectants together in calculations; reports must indicate which residual was analyzed for each sample. Chlorine dioxide acute violations are based on consecutive daily samples: if entrance sample exceeds MRDL and following‑day distribution samples (one or more of three) exceed MRDL, system is in violation, must take immediate corrective action and notify public per acute health risk procedures (subpart Q) and report to State. Failure to take the required distribution samples following an exceedance is also considered an MRDL violation and triggers required public notification and reporting.
